When Athena, disguised as an old woman, advised Arachne to show humility and ask the goddess for pardon, Arachne scornfully rejected her and challenged the goddess to a weaving contest [1]. After the competition, Athena found Arachne's work flawless but was enraged by the girl's skill and defiance [1]. Athena destroyed Arachne's web and struck her repeatedly with her shuttle [1]. Hesiod's account adds that Prometheus had also tried to trick Zeus by presenting him with bones covered in fat while offering the better meat to mortals, which angered Zeus [2][3]. Hesiod notes that Prometheus could not escape Zeus's heavy anger despite his many wiles, and he was bound with inextricable bonds and tormented by the eagle until Heracles eventually freed him [3][4].

Odysseus escaped Polyphemus through a two-part plan. First, he blinded the Cyclops by sharpening a wooden club, heating it in fire, and driving it into Polyphemus's eye with the help of his comrades [1][2]. When Polyphemus called out to other Cyclopes for help, they misunderstood his cries of "Nobody" and departed [1][2]. Second, after the blinded Cyclops opened the cave door to let his sheep out to pasture, Odysseus tied the sheep together in groups of three and hid himself underneath the largest ram by clinging to its fleece [1][2]. He and his comrades escaped with the sheep, and once at the ships, Odysseus shouted his name to the Cyclops as they sailed away [1][2].

responses_by_run.answer: Achilles died by being struck with an arrow. According to Homer, he was fated to be slain by a god and a mortal [1], and Hector, dying, foretold that Achilles would be slain by Paris and Phoebus Apollo at the Scaean gate [2]. Ovid describes how Paris shot an arrow at Achilles, guided by Apollo, at Apollo's and Neptune's instigation [3], though Ovid also records an alternative account in which Achilles was killed by Paris and Apollo with arrows [4]. Apollodorus notes that Achilles would die by the hand of Apollo [5], which came to pass after he killed Tenes despite a forewarning from his mother Thetis [6]. Homer's account indicates that Thetis foretold her son would perish beneath the wall of the Trojans by the swift missiles of Apollo [7], and that his death would follow soon after Hector's death [8].

responses_by_run.answer: Achilles withdrew from fighting after his quarrel with Agamemnon because the commander took his prize of honor, Briseis. According to Homer, Achilles was angered that Agamemnon threatened to seize his prize despite Achilles bearing the brunt of the fierce battle [1]. In response to this dishonor, Achilles declared he would return home to Phthia rather than remain dishonored and continue to pile up riches for Agamemnon [1]. Apollodorus similarly reports that Achilles did not go forth to war because he was angry on account of Briseis, the daughter of Chryses the priest [2].

Athena turned Arachne into a spider as punishment for her pride and defiance [1]. Arachne was a mortal weaver of extraordinary skill who refused to acknowledge Athena's superiority in the art of weaving [1]. When Athena, disguised as an old woman, advised Arachne to show humility and ask the goddess for pardon, Arachne scornfully rejected her and challenged the goddess to a weaving contest [1]. After Arachne lost the contest, Athena destroyed her work in rage at Arachne's skill and struck her repeatedly [2]. When Arachne attempted suicide in response to this insult, Athena saved her life but transformed her into a spider, condemning her to weave forever as eternal punishment for her presumption in rivaling a goddess [3].

Prometheus was punished for two main transgressions: stealing fire and giving it to humans [1][2][3], and for attempting to deceive Zeus during a dispute at Mecone by dividing sacrificial portions unfairly [2][3]. When Zeus discovered that Prometheus had hidden fire in a stalk of fennel and given it to mankind, Zeus ordered Hephaestus to bind Prometheus to Mount Caucasus with inextricable bonds and set an eagle upon him to devour his liver daily, which would regenerate each night [1]. This severe punishment lasted many years until Heracles eventually released him [1].

Odysseus escaped Polyphemus through a two-part plan. First, he blinded the Cyclops by sharpening a wooden club, heating it in fire, and driving it into Polyphemus's eye with the help of his comrades [1][2]. When Polyphemus cried out for help from other Cyclopes, they misunderstood his cries of "Nobody" and left him alone [1][2]. Second, after the blinding, Odysseus tied the Cyclops's rams together in groups of three and had his men cling to the middle ram of each group, while he himself clung to the largest ram [1][2]. When Polyphemus opened the cave door in the morning to let his flocks out to pasture, he felt the sheep as they passed but could not detect the men hidden beneath them [1][2]. Odysseus and his comrades thus escaped with the sheep to their ships [1][2].

At the wedding of Peleus and Thetis, the gods celebrated the marriage with feast and song on Mount Pelion [1]. The marriage itself followed Peleus's forceful seizure of Thetis, during which he held her fast as she resisted through shape-shifting, transforming into fire, water, and various beasts until she resumed her original form [1]. As wedding gifts, Chiron gave Peleus an ashen spear [1], and Poseidon gave him immortal horses named Balius and Xanthus [1].

Demeter stopped the crops from growing because she was grieving over the abduction of her daughter [1]. She vowed that she would never let fruit spring out of the ground until she beheld her own fair-faced daughter with her eyes [1]. She was so wrathful in her heart that no one of the blessed gods, despite their pleas and offers of gifts, was able to persuade her to change her mind [2].

    WHERE e.name ILIKE 'Perseus'

      AND encounters.depth < 20
)

responses_by_run.answer: Zeus's lineage traces back through several divine generations to primordial chaos. Zeus was the son of Cronus [1] and Rhea [2]. Cronus himself was born from Earth (Gaia) and Ouranos [3], who represent the foundational divine pair in Greek cosmology. Earth and Ouranos emerged from the primordial forces, with their union producing the Titans, of whom Cronus was the most prominent [3]. This genealogy establishes Zeus's descent from the earliest divine entities recognized in Greek mythology, connecting the king of the gods to the fundamental cosmic principles from which all divinity originated.

ORDER BY h.name ASC

responses_by_run.answer: Achilles' divine lineage to Zeus follows a clear patrilineal descent. Zeus fathered Aeacus with Aegina [1]. Aeacus then had a son Peleus with his wife Endeis [1]. Peleus married Thetis, a Nereid (sea goddess), and together they became the parents of Achilles [1]. Thus Achilles descends from Zeus through his grandfather Aeacus and his father Peleus, while also possessing divine blood through his mother Thetis [1]. Homer's Iliad presents Achilles himself asserting this lineage, stating 'The father that begat me is one that is lord among the many Myrmidons, even Peleus, son of Aeacus; and Aeacus was begotten of Zeus,' emphasizing that his connection to Zeus makes him mightier than those of merely mortal or river descent [2].

The Homeric Hymns also describe her as the daughter of Zeus [5]. Additionally, Hesiod offers a distinct origin story, stating that Aphrodite was born from the sea foam formed by the severed members of Heaven, which Cronus had cast into the sea [6]. Ovid similarly identifies her as a child of Zeus [7].
